title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Ability Bias






Ability Bias


Ability bias: higher-ability people choose more schooling but would earn higher wages even without schooling

OLS estimate reflects both the return to schooling and the return to ability
Ability bias is thought to be positive → OLS overestimates the return to schooling

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Ability Bias
Suppose the true earnings equation is:
\[\ln Y = \beta_{0} + \beta_1 schl + \beta_2 abil + \epsilon\]
Where \(\epsilon\) has \(E[\epsilon \mid schl, abil] = 0\)
Assume schooling increases with ability:
\[abil = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 schl + v\]
with \(v\) uncorrelated with \(schl\)

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Ability Bias
If we estimate a regression omitting ability:
\[\ln Y = \tilde{\beta}_1 schl + e\]
The OLS coefficient on schooling equals:
\[\tilde{\beta}_s = \frac{Cov(lnY, s)}{Var(s)}\]

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Ability Bias
Plug \(\ln Y = \beta_1 schl + \beta_2 abil + \epsilon\) into the formula for \(\tilde{\beta}_s\):
\[\tilde{\beta}_s = \frac{Cov(\beta_{0} + \beta_1 schl + \beta_2 abil + \epsilon, schl)}{Var(schl)}\]
Because \(\beta_0\) is constant and \(\epsilon\) is uncorrelated with \(schl\):
\[\tilde{\beta}_s = \frac{\beta_1 Var(schl) + \beta_2 Cov(abil, schl)}{Var(schl)} = \beta_1 + \beta_2 \alpha_1\]

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Ability Bias






The Bias Formula


\[\tilde{\beta}_s = \underbrace{\beta_1}_{\text{true return}} + \underbrace{\beta_2 \alpha_1}_{\text{ability bias}}\]
The ability bias \(\beta_2 \alpha_1\) depends on:

\(\beta_2\): the earnings return to ability
\(\alpha_1\): the relationship between ability and schooling

If both are positive → ability bias is positive → OLS overestimates the return to schooling

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Addressing Ability Bias
Economists have developed methods to address ability bias:
Twin Studies:

Compare earnings of identical twins with different schooling levels
Presumably, twins have the same level of ability — comparing them avoids ability bias

Instrumental Variables (IV):

Method that isolates variation in schooling unrelated to ability
E.g., changes in compulsory schooling laws, proximity to university
These changes affect schooling but are unrelated to ability

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Twin Studies






Ashenfelter and Rouse (1998)



Used data on identical twins in the US (collected at a Twins festival)
OLS estimate: biased return of about 11% per year
Twin differences estimate: return of about 7% per year
Suggests ability bias of about 4 percentage points

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Compulsory Schooling

Another method: use changes in compulsory schooling laws as an instrument for schooling
Several US states have a minimum school leaving age (generally around 16 years old)
Students born earlier in the year can leave school earlier

Someone born in January can leave earlier than someone born in December of the same year
On average, people born later in the year have more schooling

Angrist and Krueger (1991) use this variation to estimate returns to schooling

Estimate a return of about 7–10% per year of schooling

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Compulsory Schooling

Canada has maximum school entry laws and minimum school leaving laws

Over time, students mandated to enter school earlier and leave later
This increases average schooling levels, unrelated to ability

Oreopoulos (2006) uses this variation to estimate returns to schooling in Canada

Finds that an additional year of compulsory schooling increases earnings by about 7–12%

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text: Compulsory Schooling

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Signalling

All studies cited so far have attributed returns to schooling to human capital accumulation
Some studies have attempted to separate human capital from signalling effects
Ferrer and Riddell (2002) use Canadian data to estimate credential effects

Look at people with same years of schooling, but different credentials
E.g., someone with a high school diploma versus someone with the same years but did not graduate

Find that obtaining the credential does matter — consistent with some signalling

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Discussion
Twin studies and IV studies both estimate returns to schooling of about 7–10%, which is lower than the OLS estimate. Does this mean ability bias is the whole story, or could there be biases working in the opposite direction that partially offset it?

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Social Returns to Education

Most discussion so far has focused on private returns to education (returns to the individual)
We know there are positive externalities to society as a whole:

States/provinces with higher average education have higher earnings in excess of the private return
More highly educated immigrants in STEM have a positive effect on productivity of other workers
More highly educated populations have lower crime rates, better health outcomes, more civic participation








Policy Implication


Because social returns exceed private returns, there is a rationale for public subsidies to education

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Education and Inequality

Earnings inequality has increased in many countries over the past few decades
In Canada:

Rose over the 80s and 90s
Has been stable since


Two sources of rising inequality:

Returns to schooling: college premium has grown
Inequality within education groups: growing wage dispersion even among equally-educated workers

In Canada, much of the rise is related to inequality within education groups

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text: Education and Inequality

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text: Education and Inequality

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Education and Inequality
Why has the return to education increased?
Skill-Biased Technological Change:

New technologies increase demand for skilled workers
Increases the wage premium for higher education
Thought to be the major driver in the 1980s

Globalization:

Increased trade and outsourcing
Reduces demand for lower-skilled workers locally

Institutional Changes:

Decline in unionization, changes in labour market policies
Negatively affects bargaining power of lower-skilled workers

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Introduction

Formal schooling is one way to develop human capital
Another important way is through job training







Types of Training



General Training: skills that are useful at many firms
Specific Training: skills that are only useful at a specific firm




Training helps develop skills that increase human capital — in this section we evaluate the economics of job training

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Who Pays for Job Training

It is not uncommon for firms to pay for job training

Some companies provide training to all employees
Others fund things like MBA programs

Under what circumstances would the firm pay versus the individual?
The answer differs for general versus specific training

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Who Pays for Job Training
General training: employees fund training themselves

General training increases productivity at many firms

Employees can take skills to other firms

Firms offer higher wages to employees with general training (very similar to schooling)
But employees fund the training themselves

Pay for it as long as lifetime wage increase exceeds the cost of training

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Who Pays for Job Training





 













General training illustrated:

Without training: employee earns wage \(W_a\) (equals VMP without training)
Employee who gets training:

Earns lower wage \(VMP_t\) during training
Earns higher wage \(VMP^*\) after training

Worth it for employee if present value of wage increase exceeds cost of training

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Who Pays for Job Training
Specific training: firms pay

Specific training only increases productivity at one firm

Skills not transferable to other firms

Company would pay if benefits exceed costs

Benefits: higher productivity of employee
Costs: wages paid during training period

Would not have to pay higher wages — there is no competition for workers with this specific skill

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Who Pays for Job Training





 













Specific training illustrated:

Before and after training: employee earns wage \(W_a\)
Firm costs during training: \(W_a - VMP_t\)
Firm benefits after training: \(VMP^* - W_a\)
Worth it if present value of benefits exceeds present value of costs

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Who Pays for Job Training
Shared investment — happens when there is a risk of the individual leaving after training:

Firms pay below \(W_a\) during the training period (but still above the VMP during training)
Pay above \(W_a\) after training (but below the employee’s VMP)
In this way, employee and employer share the costs and benefits

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Who Pays for Job Training





 













Shared specific training:
During training period:

Employee cost: earning less than \(W_a\)
Employer cost: paying above VMP

After training period:

Employee benefit: earning more than \(W_a\)
Employer benefit: paying below VMP

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Who Pays for Job Training

For illustrative purposes, we have depicted training as a one-time event

In reality, training is often ongoing throughout a worker’s career
Workers may receive multiple types of training at different times
Firms may have formal training programs or informal on-the-job training

A more gradual training leads to smoother curves — but the lesson is still the same

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Who Pays for Job Training





 













Gradual shared training:

Lesson is still the same
Costs gradually fall over time during training
Benefits gradually grow
Worth it for employer and employee if benefits exceed costs

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Training and Government
Governments often subsidize job training programs. Several rationales for public funding:

Positive externalities from a more productive workforce
Individuals may underinvest due to credit constraints
Imperfect information about training benefits

Some current government funding initiatives:

Canada-Ontario Job Grant: funds businesses to train employees
NPower Canada: registered charity providing tech training, funded by government

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Training and Government

An active area of labour economics is program evaluation — evaluating the effectiveness of government training programs
In some cases, people are randomly allocated to training programs

Can directly compare outcomes of those who received training to those who did not
Identifies the causal effect of training

In most cases, people self-select into training programs

People in training and comparison groups differ in many ways besides training
Makes it difficult to isolate the effect of training itself

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Training and Government
Program evaluation uses econometric techniques to address selection issues:

Difference-in-Differences (DiD): compare changes in outcomes over time between treatment and control groups
Propensity Score Matching (PSM): match individuals in treatment and control groups based on observable characteristics
Instrumental Variables (IV): use external factors that affect training participation but not outcomes directly







Evidence from Program Evaluation



U.S. training programs have positive results for young women from poorer backgrounds
But no effect for men
More successful programs emphasize human capital investment over job search assistance

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Think About It
A tech company pays for an employee’s MBA degree. Under the general vs. specific training framework, who should pay for this training, and why? What does it suggest if the firm requires the employee to stay for two years after completing the degree?

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Summary

Education is an investment in human capital — increases productivity and earnings potential
The Human Capital model explains schooling decisions based on costs and benefits

People invest in schooling until marginal benefit equals marginal cost

The Signalling model emphasizes education as a signal of ability

Education reveals productivity to employers rather than creating it

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Summary

Empirical estimates of returns to schooling are around 7–10% per year

Ability bias may lead to overestimation; twin and IV studies correct for this

Job training is another important way to develop human capital

General training funded by workers; specific training funded by firms; often shared

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Goals of This Section
In this section we will:

Discuss trends in male-female earnings differentials in Canada
Introduce taste-based and statistical discrimination theories
Explain supply-side and non-competitive theories of discrimination
Learn the Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition to measure discrimination
Review policies to address gender discrimination

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text: Male and Female Earnings

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text: Male and Female Earnings

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text: Male and Female Earnings

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Male and Female Earnings

Clearly men and women earn different amounts on average
There are two broad explanations for this gap:

Differences in characteristics (education, experience, occupation, industry, hours worked, etc.)
Differences in returns to those characteristics (discrimination)

Our models so far have not left room for discrimination

We treated all workers as the same
So there should not be any differences in returns

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Male and Female Earnings
In this section, we explore economic theories of discrimination:

Can come from employers, customers, co-workers
Can be statistical or taste-based

Estimating discrimination empirically is difficult:

Need to control for all relevant characteristics
Need to separate differences in characteristics from differences in returns

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Male and Female Earnings
Methods that can help:

Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition
Audit studies
Field experiments

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Discussion
The gender earnings gap has narrowed over time but has not closed. Why might we observe a persistent gap even as women’s educational attainment has surpassed men’s in many countries?

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Demand-Side Theories
Demand-side theories focus on the behaviour of employers in demanding labour. Discrimination can happen for various reasons:

Pure prejudice against female workers
Customer preference to buy from male workers
Male workers’ aversion to working with women







Warning


These all cause a fall in the demand for women relative to men in the labour market — reducing wages and employment of female workers

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Taste-Based Discrimination






Becker (1957)


Taste-based discrimination: employers have a “taste” for discrimination — they behave as if hiring women is more costly than it actually is




Firms produce according to: \(y = f(N_m + N_w)\)
In a competitive market, profits are: \[ \pi = p \cdot f(N_m + N_w) - w_m N_m - w_f N_w \]
Firms do not maximize profit strictly, but instead maximize: \[ U = \pi - d \cdot N_w \]

\(d\) measures the degree of discrimination
If \(d = 0\): no discrimination; if \(d > 0\): firms get disutility from hiring women

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Taste-Based Discrimination
The first order conditions for utility maximization are:
\[ p \cdot MP_{N_m} = w_m \] \[ p \cdot MP_{N_w} = w_f + d \]

For both men and women, firms hire up to where VMP equals the effective cost of hiring
But for women, there is an additional cost \(d\) due to discrimination
If \(w_m = w_f\) and men and women are equally productive, this implies firms hire fewer women

Discrimination drives a wedge between wages and the MRP

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Taste-Based Discrimination





 














Graph plots labour demand for women
Discrimination shifts demand curve left
Without discrimination: firm hires where \(w_f = MRP_{ND}\)
With discrimination: firm hires where \(w_f + d = MRP_D\)

Or equivalently \(w_f = MRP_D - d\)

Implies a lower level of female labour

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Taste-Based Discrimination

Above analysis is for a single employer
Employers discriminate along a spectrum — some have a high \(d\), some have a low or no \(d\)
Suppose women are able to seek out the non-discriminating employers
If we order firms from lowest to highest by the amount of discrimination:

We can get the market demand curve by summing individual demand curves horizontally

This demand curve is plotted on the next slide

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Taste-Based Discrimination





 














Vertical axis is the ratio of female to male wages
For non-discriminating firms, this ratio is 1

A certain set of firms will hire women at this ratio (flat portion of demand curve)

As the supply of women grows, they must work at more discriminating firms

These firms will only hire when the wage ratio falls

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Taste-Based Discrimination





 














If the supply of female labour is small enough, they can work at non-discriminating firms

Wage ratio is 1

With a larger supply, some will have to work at discriminating firms

Wage ratio falls below 1
This is where the demand curve slopes downwards
Wage gap emerges

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Think About It
In Becker’s model, discriminating firms sacrifice profits by not hiring equally productive women at lower wages. What would happen to taste-based discrimination in the long run if product markets are perfectly competitive?

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Statistical Discrimination






Statistical Discrimination


Statistical discrimination: firms use group characteristics to infer individual productivity

Arises because of imperfect information — employers do not know individual worker productivity perfectly
Instead they use signals to infer worker quality
If one group has lower average productivity (or a noisier signal), firms may pay them less on average





Contrast with taste-based discrimination, which relies on employers having overt prejudice

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Statistical Discrimination: Theory
Assume that the abilities of male and female workers are distributed with means \(\bar{a}_{m}\) and \(\bar{a}_{f}\). The firm has access to a signal of ability \(x\) for each person. Expected ability is:
\[a(x) = \bar{a} + \alpha (x - \bar{a})\]
Where \(\alpha\) is the reliability of the signal:

If \(\alpha = 0\): the signal provides no information beyond the average
If \(\alpha = 1\): the signal is perfectly informative

Workers are paid a wage equal to their marginal revenue product

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Statistical Discrimination
Paying workers their marginal revenue product implies:
\[w(x) = p a(x) = p \bar{a} + p \alpha (x - \bar{a})\]
Assume \(\bar{a}_{m} = \bar{a}_{f}\) (men and women are equally productive on average), but the signal is more reliable for men: \(\alpha_m > \alpha_f\)
Differences arise between workers who score the same on the signal:

If a man and woman score above average (\(x - \bar{a} > 0\)), then men are paid more
If a man and woman score below average (\(x - \bar{a} < 0\)), then women are paid more

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Statistical Discrimination





 










Male line is steeper because the signal is more reliable (\(\alpha_m > \alpha_f\))
For test scores above average: men are paid more
For test scores below average: women are paid more
At the average: they are paid the same

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Statistical Discrimination

There are no underlying differences between males and females

Differences in wages arise because of differences in the quality of the signal
Firms place more weight on average ability for female workers
Firms place more weight on the actual signal for male workers

But where does the assumption \(\alpha_m > \alpha_f\) come from?

Possibly related to prejudicial attitudes of firms
Some believe standardized tests favour males

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Statistical Discrimination

There may also be differences in \(\bar{a}_m\) and \(\bar{a}_f\)

Possibly due to pre-market discrimination leading to lower human capital among women

In this case, males are paid more at every signal level
Wage differences do not necessarily arise from overt discrimination

They may originate in differences in information signals or average productivity
But it is difficult to explain why such differences in signal quality exist

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Think About It
Under statistical discrimination, a high-ability woman and a high-ability man both score well on an employment test, but the signal is noisier for women. What would happen to the wage gap between these two workers if the employer could conduct a longer, more thorough evaluation of all candidates?

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Statistical Discrimination





 










In this graph the quality of the signal is the same (equal slopes)
But there are differences in average productivity

Male line lies above female line

Men will be paid more because of the average difference

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Supply-Side Theories

We discussed demand-side theories — focused on employer behaviour
Discrimination may also arise on the labour supply side

Factors that affect where women choose or are able to work

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Crowding Hypothesis






Crowding Hypothesis


Women are overrepresented in certain occupations, pushing up their labour supply in those occupations — which depresses wages relative to men

Women are paid their marginal product
But are corralled into a small set of jobs, which depresses wages

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Dual Labour Market Theory






Dual Labour Market Theory


There are two distinct labour markets:

Primary market: high wages, good working conditions, opportunities for advancement; unionized, stable, expanding
Secondary market: low wages, poor working conditions, little opportunity for advancement; non-unionized, highly competitive, declining




Theory posits that women are concentrated in the secondary market — prejudice prevents women from entering the primary market

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Lower Reservation Wages
Theory: female reservation wages are lower because:

Costly to search for non-discriminating employers
Job search is limited by strong household ties
Ability to negotiate higher pay limited by lower threat of leaving







Note


With a lower reservation wage, women are more likely to be paid less — contributing to the pay gap
Some empirical evidence supports this

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Risk Aversion

Large literature documenting that women are less aggressive/competitive in bargaining

Also less confident in their abilities
Evidence of this in many studies in economics and psychology

Might mean women are less likely to compete for higher paying jobs

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Differences in Preferences
May be differences in preferences for education, training, hours, work conditions, occupation — all of these are correlated with pay






The Endogeneity Problem


These choices are sometimes a product of discrimination — so it is hard to separate preferences from discrimination effects
Example: STEM fields pay well, but are male dominated — history of discrimination in this field may lead women not to choose it

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Non-Competitive Theories

One issue with the above theories: they assume competitive markets
Men and women are assumed to have equal productivity
Discriminating firms hire fewer women because of prejudice
But non-discriminating firms can hire more women at lower wages

Would increase their profits
Non-discriminating firms would bid up wages of women
Should close the gap

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Non-Competitive Theories






Why Does the Gap Persist?


Non-competitive theories explain persistent wage gaps when markets are not perfectly competitive — due to monopsony power, imperfect information, search frictions, etc.

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Imperfect Information

Even if firms know they can increase profits by hiring more women, they might not be able to immediately change their workforce

Hiring and recruiting are costly — search frictions, quasi-fixed costs

Firms may be slow to adjust to profit opportunities
This can lead to persistent wage gaps

But does not explain why the gaps have persisted for so long

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Queueing Theory

Some firms pay efficiency wages

Wages above the market clearing level to increase productivity

This results in a queue of workers wanting to work at the firm
While rationing jobs, firms may discriminate

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Political Pressure

Sometimes market decisions are overridden by political pressures
A male-centric government or union may:

Hire more men in government jobs
Be discriminatory with education and training

The political pressure could come from interest groups

May have significant resources to lobby the government

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Monopsony Power

Monopsony gives firms power to set wages below competitive levels
Monopsonies may take advantage of the relative immobility of women to lower their wages

Recall women may have stronger ties to household

They may also try to pit men and women against each other

Create competition between the groups to lower wages

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Systemic Discrimination






Systemic Discrimination


Discrimination is embedded in social and economic systems — has been going on for so long that it is now self-perpetuating
Could come from:

Existence of “old boys” mentality
Old job requirements that implicitly discriminate but continue to exist

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Productivity Differences

It may be the case that men and women have productivity differences

This could determine pay differences even in competitive markets

Note: not innate productivity differences
Differences coming from acquisition of human capital over time:

Education
Training
Work experience

If human capital investments are a choice, then pay differences are not discrimination
But it could be that choices are influenced by discrimination

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Dual Role

Traditionally women have more of a dual role than men — balancing household and market work
If this continues to be true, then women:

Have less continuity in work (mainly from interruptions for children)
Are more likely to have periods of paid work and labour force withdrawals

This leads to lower accumulation of human capital

Because there is less time to recoup the costs

In some sense this is a rational choice — but is rooted in a society that does not accommodate enough for working mothers

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Pre-Market Discrimination






Pre-Market Discrimination


Pre-market discrimination: discrimination that influences choices before workers even enter the labour market

Education
Training
Career path

What looks like a rational choice is itself affected by discrimination



Example: STEM jobs pay well but are male dominated — women are discouraged from entering these fields, and thus do not have access to the higher pay that comes with them

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Introduction

Now that we have discussed theories of discrimination, how do we measure it?
Difficult because in most cases discrimination is not directly observable

There is no “discrimination” variable in datasets

Can design experiments to measure discrimination:

Audit studies
Field experiments

But in most cases we have to rely on observational data

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Introduction

Measuring discrimination involves comparing people of equal productivity

So that any leftover wage differences could be due to discrimination

But we do not observe productivity directly
Instead, hold constant variables related to productivity:

Education
Experience
Occupation
Industry
Hours worked

Then decompose the wage difference into part due to characteristics and part due to other factors

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition






Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition


Method to decompose differences in average earnings between two groups into:

Explained part: due to differences in characteristics (endowments)
Unexplained part: due to differences in returns to those characteristics (potentially discrimination)




Suppose we estimate a regression of log earnings on observed characteristics for men and women:
\[ \ln(Y_m) =\hat\beta_m \cdot \bar{X}_m \]
\[ \ln(Y_f) =\hat\beta_f \cdot \bar{X}_f \]

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition
The difference in average log earnings is:
\[ \ln(Y_m) - \ln(Y_f) = \hat\beta_m \cdot \bar{X}_m - \hat\beta_f \cdot \bar{X}_f \]
Add and subtract \(\hat\beta_m \cdot \bar{X}_f\):
\[ \ln(Y_m) - \ln(Y_f) = \underbrace{\hat\beta_m \cdot (\bar{X}_m - \bar{X}_f)}_{\text{explained}} + \underbrace{\bar{X}_f \cdot (\hat\beta_m - \hat\beta_f)}_{\text{unexplained}} \]

Explained: holds slope constant at \(\hat\beta_m\), looks at differences in average \(X\)
Unexplained: holds average characteristics constant at \(\bar{X}_f\), looks at differences in slopes (returns)

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition






Warning


Traditionally, the unexplained part is interpreted as discrimination — but could also be due to unobserved productivity differences

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text: Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition
Suppose we have run the following regression separately for men and women:
\[\ln Y  = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{Educ} + \beta_2 \text{Experience}\]
Estimated coefficients:

Men: \(\beta^M = (2.0,\; 0.10,\; 0.02)\)
Women: \(\beta^F = (1.8,\; 0.08,\; 0.015)\)

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition
Mean observed characteristics:

Men: \(\bar{\text{Educ}}_M = 14\), \(\bar{\text{Exp}}_M = 15\)
Women: \(\bar{\text{Educ}}_F = 13\), \(\bar{\text{Exp}}_F = 12\)

Average predicted log wage for men:
\[\bar{\ln Y}_M = 2.0 + 0.10 \cdot 14 + 0.02 \cdot 15 = 2.0 + 1.4 + 0.3 = 3.7\]

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition
Average predicted log wage for women:
\[\bar{\ln Y}_F = 1.8 + 0.08 \cdot 13 + 0.015 \cdot 12 = 1.8 + 1.04 + 0.18 = 3.02\]
The wage gap is therefore:
\[\bar{\ln Y}_M - \bar{\ln Y}_F = 3.70 - 3.02 = 0.68\]
This says that the wage gap is about 0.68 log points — roughly 97% higher wages for men

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition
We decompose: \(\bar{\ln Y}_M - \bar{\ln Y}_F = \text{Explained} + \text{Unexplained}\)
Explained (due to characteristics):
\[\text{Explained} = (\bar{X}_M - \bar{X}_F)\beta^M\]
Differences in means: Education: \(14 - 13 = 1\), Experience: \(15 - 12 = 3\)
\[\text{Explained} = 1 \cdot 0.10 + 3 \cdot 0.02 = 0.10 + 0.06 = 0.16\]
About \(0.16\) log points of the gap are due to men having more education and experience.

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition
Unexplained (returns to characteristics):
\[\text{Unexplained (slopes)} = \bar{X}_F \left(\beta_M - \beta_F\right)\]
Coefficient differences: Education: \(0.10 - 0.08 = 0.02\), Experience: \(0.02 - 0.015 = 0.005\)
\[\text{Unexplained (slopes)} = 13 \cdot 0.02 + 12 \cdot 0.005 = 0.26 + 0.06 = 0.32\]
Intercept difference: \(\beta_{0M} - \beta_{0F} = 2.0 - 1.8 = 0.20\)
Total unexplained: \(0.32 + 0.20 = 0.52\)

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition






Final Decomposition


\[0.68 = \underbrace{0.16}_{\text{explained (24\%)}} + \underbrace{0.52}_{\text{unexplained (76\%)}}\]

Explained (\(0.16\), ~24%): due to men having higher average education and experience
Unexplained (\(0.52\), ~76%): due to different returns to characteristics and intercept differences

text:
Blinder-Oaxaca Decomposition
Here is an example using real data from Canada:

Labour Force Survey from September 2025
Restricted to people aged 35–54 with wages > 0
First examine summary statistics, then run a regular regression, then the decomposition

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Collider Bias

Sometimes researchers control for variables in a regression to adjust the wage gap

What is the gap if we hold constant age, education, experience, occupation, industry, hours worked, etc.?

The idea is to compare people who are the same on all relevant characteristics







Collider Bias


Collider bias: controlling for certain variables (like occupation) can actually create bias in discrimination estimates if those variables are themselves outcomes of discrimination

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Collider Bias
Example — the tech industry:

Men and women have equal ability in the general population
Women face discrimination in tech, so to get the job they must have very high ability
Men can enter even with moderate ability
If you look at the wage gap in tech jobs, it might appear to favour women

In the same occupation, women will have higher ability because they had to overcome discrimination
Comparing men and women within occupation creates ability bias

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Collider Bias





 













This happened at Google:

There was a complaint that women were being underpaid
An analysis found that men were underpaid
A perfect example of collider bias

They looked within jobs
Women of very high ability were selected into those jobs
Their wages were higher because of that

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Collider Bias
How to avoid collider bias:






Best Practice


Do not add variables that are outcomes of discrimination to the regression

Occupation is often an outcome of discrimination
Industry may also be an outcome

Instead include only predetermined characteristics: things that are not affected by discrimination — mainly basic demographics, possibly education and experience

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Discussion
In a Blinder-Oaxaca decomposition, the unexplained component is often interpreted as discrimination. Why might this interpretation overstate or understate the true amount of discrimination?

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Introduction

Significant statistical work has been done on this issue

Why? Its importance and availability of data

We will briefly review some of the evidence here, with a focus on Canadian studies

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Evidence
Key findings:

Women in Canada earn about 60% of what men earn (unconditional gap)
After controlling for characteristics, the gap shrinks to about 85%
Pay gap is smaller in the public sector — pay practices are more egalitarian in government
Gap has been falling over time — many factors could contribute
Internationally, gaps are smaller with stronger bargaining structures
Gap is smaller the more competitive the industry

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Evidence
Additional findings:

Occupational segregation does not explain a large part of the gap

Gap is explained more by industry than occupation

Women face career penalties from family responsibilities
Glass ceilings are an observed phenomenon

At the top end of the pay distribution, gaps are larger
Lots of international evidence of differences in career advancement

Unions have a higher impact on women than men

Offset by the fact that women are less likely to be unionized

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Evidence

Mixed evidence on job-protected leave

Leave is good because it protects jobs for women
But might make employers less likely to hire women in the first place
Evidence shows it lowers wages for women in the U.S.
In Canada it increases job continuity

Some evidence that gap grows with more work experience

Upon initial entry, gap is small
Grows over time

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Introduction

The same techniques used to analyze gender wage gaps can be used to estimate gaps for other groups
This is usually done by race or ethnicity

U.S. studies have focused in particular on racial discrimination

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Evidence for Other Groups
Indigenous peoples in Canada:

About 85% of non-Indigenous wages off reserve
Shrinks after controlling for characteristics

Ethnic-white wage gaps in Canada:

Complicated by the fact that many non-white Canadians are also immigrants
Immigration has its own independent effect on wages
Controlling for this, gaps are very high — summarized on next slide

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text: Evidence for Other Groups

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Evidence for Other Groups
Evidence in the U.S.:

Large literature on Black-white wage gaps — about 68% of white wages

Shrinks when controlling for past test scores (measure of pre-market productivity)
Pre-market discrimination also plays a large role
Large component of discrimination remains

Gaps favour Chinese and Southeast Asian workers — not the same in Canada

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Discussion
If you were designing a single policy to reduce the gender pay gap, would you target demand-side discrimination (e.g., employer behaviour) or supply-side factors (e.g., occupational choice, human capital accumulation)? Why?

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Introduction

Gender discrimination has been an issue for a long time
Several policies are enacted to combat it:

Equal pay
Equal employment opportunity
Policies to facilitate female employment

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Equal Pay
Pay equity: requires that jobs which are substantially similar receive equal pay

Looks at very similar jobs; minor differences are allowed
Issue: deals with similar jobs in similar establishments — does not address equity issues across jobs/industries

Equal pay for equal work: broadens the scope

Assigns points to jobs based on skill, effort, responsibility, working conditions
Jobs with similar points should receive similar pay
Can apply to different occupations, but still in same firm/industry

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Equal Pay

Applies only to jobs that are predominantly male or female (>70%) — pay in female-dominated jobs adjusted to that of male-dominated jobs

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Equal Pay





 













Equal pay for equal work example:

Pay plotted against point scores
In this example, male dominated jobs have generally higher pay
Solutions could be:

Raise female line to male line
Raise female pay to male pay point-by-point for similar scores
Raise female points to male line at each point value

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Equal Pay






Note


Equal pay for equal work is based on administrative concept of value (points for skill, effort, responsibility, working conditions) — not based on economic (market) value

This is purposeful: market value reflects discrimination; administrative value tries to remove this

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Equal Employment Opportunity

Equal pay focused on equalizing wages
Equal employment opportunity focuses on equalizing access to jobs

But by equalizing access, we also expect wages to equalize

Key initiative is affirmative action (aka employment equity)

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Equal Employment Opportunity






Affirmative Action


Generally involves preferential treatment for minority groups

Intended to overcome past and current discrimination
Designed to be used temporarily to restore balance

In Canada:

Applies only to federal workforce (~10% of jobs)
Applies to four targeted groups: women, visible minorities, disabled persons, indigenous peoples
Continues to be very controversial

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Facilitating Policies
Finally, there are policies that can help facilitate women in the workforce:

Parental leave
Child care subsidies
Flexible work arrangements

Canada has done well on the first two — expansion of child care subsidies recently is a good example

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Facilitating Policies

Some consider expanding unionization to be a facilitating policy

Unions bargain for greater pay and working conditions
Expanding this to cover more women would help
May also generate more power for women to argue for other types of legislation

Removing pay secrecy can also help

If employees know what others are paid, they can better negotiate
Pay secrecy tends to hide discrimination
Some jurisdictions have passed laws banning pay secrecy

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Preference and Attitudes

We saw that discrimination in part is due to preferences and attitudes

Taste-based discrimination is one example

Could use public policy to try to change these attitudes:

Public awareness campaigns
Education programs

Not clear how well this works

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Introduction

We have outlined the different anti-discrimination policies
How effective are these policies?
Relatively straightforward to analyze statistically

Use Program Evaluation techniques
Data generally available

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Pay Equity






Pay Equity Effectiveness



Generally ineffective in closing the gender gap
Some evidence of an impact in the UK
In the U.S., pay equity is difficult to disentangle from other civil rights legislation — effects are inconclusive

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Equal Pay for Equal Work

Analyzed mostly in the public sector
Recall the legislation is limited in scope

Male/female dominated jobs in same firm/industry

Policy shown to close about one-third of the gender gap in the public sector

Limited evidence in the private sector

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Affirmative Action

Affirmative action is most prominent in the U.S.
Several studies have examined its effect:

Evidence that it helped employment opportunities of Black men

Were the main targets of the legislation in earlier years

In later years, helped both Black men and women

Targets were expanded in later years

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Facilitating Policies






Evidence on Facilitating Policies



Parental leave policies help create job continuity
Subsidized child care increases female labour force participation — good evidence from Quebec
Pay transparency reduces the gender gap by about 30% in academia — using evidence from the “sunshine list” in Ontario
“Tenure clock stopping” policies reduce tenure rates for women — unintended consequence: men can increase productivity
Banning criminal history questions hurt employment of Black men — increased use of discrimination

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Summary

Discrimination can arise from tastes (Becker), statistical discrimination, supply-side factors, and non-competitive markets
Measuring discrimination is difficult because productivity is not observed

Blinder-Oaxaca decomposition is a common method

Collider bias is a potential issue when controlling for variables that are themselves outcomes of discrimination
There are a number of initiatives to reduce discrimination

Mixed evidence on their effectiveness

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Introduction

Before analyzing any market, we need the context in which people and firms decide
Institutions and legislation shape the employer–employee relationship
Rules do not just constrain behaviour — they change wages and employment

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Labour Force Participation

The first decision is whether to make yourself available for work







Key Definition


Labour Force: people in the eligible population who participate in labour market activities as either employed or unemployed




Eligible population includes

Population 15 years and over
Non-institutionalized
People not living on reserve
Civilians (non-military)

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Labour Force Participation

Eligible people who are not part of the labour force include

Retired people
People who do only unpaid work in the home
Full time students (who are 15 years old and over)
People who just give up on looking for work








Key Definition


Labour Force Participation Rate (LFPR): The share of the eligible population (POP) in the labour force (LF)



\[
LFPR = LF/POP
\]

The LFPR is a common statistic reported in the news

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text: Labour Force Participation

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text: Labour Force Participation

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Employment and Unemployment

People in the labour force are either employed or unemployed







Key Definitions


Employed (E): people who worked during the reference period

Includes people normally employed but temporarily absent

Unemployed (U): people who did not work during the reference period but

were available for work and actively looked for work in the past four weeks
were waiting to start a new job within the next four weeks
on temporary layoff and expecting to be recalled to that job





The employment rate (ER) and unemployment rate (UR) are

\[ER = E/POP\] \[UR = U/LF\]

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Goals of This Section
In this section we will:

Build the labour supply model
Derive the labour supply curve
Examine effects of labour market policies within that model

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Canada and Indigenous Peoples

Inuit, First Nations, and Métis Peoples have a special constitutional relationship with the Crown

Including “existing aboriginal and treaty rights” under section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982

Laws and policies are being reviewed against the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples







Tip


We look at contemporary effects of Canada’s historical policies in Chapter 15.

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Canada and Indigenous Peoples
Which rules apply at work?

Employment relationships follow the same legislation as everyone else, depending on industry

Federal jurisdiction covers band councils and Indigenous self-governments


Taxation:

Employment income may be tax exempt when the work is substantially “situated on a reserve” and done by a registered First Nations individual

Section 87 of the Indian Act

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Federal and Provincial Jurisdiction

The British North America Act of 1867 divided power between the two levels of government
Which government regulates your job depends on what industry you work in, not where you live

Federal jurisdiction covers the federal public service plus a short list of industries:

Interprovincial and international transportation
Telecommunications and broadcasting
Banks — but not credit unions
Postal and courier services

The provinces have everything else — the large majority of workers.

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Federal and Provincial Jurisdiction

The provinces have responsibility for everything else

This is the large majority of workers

Responsibilities overlap in places

The federal government helps fund health care and education
But the province has exclusive responsibility for managing those sectors








Why This Matters


Two workers doing similar jobs can face completely different employment law depending on their employer’s industry.

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
The Canada Labour Code






Key Definition


The Canada Labour Code (CLC) sets labour standards for industries under federal responsibility. It has four parts.




Part I — Industrial Relations: collective bargaining and unionization
Part II — Occupational Health and Safety
Part III — Labour Standards: employment conditions and protections
Part IV — Penalties and procedures for noncompliant employers

Not every part applies to every worker: federal private sector gets all four, the federal public sector only II and IV.

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
The Canada Labour Code
Not every part applies to every worker:

Federal private sector workers — all four parts
Federal public sector — only Parts II and IV
Territories, private sector and municipal employees — only Part I

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Provincial Employment Standards

Each province has an Employment Standards Act or Code setting rules on:

Minimum wages, vacation time, parental and sick leave
Termination of employment, limits on hours

We care because these rules change the decisions of workers and firms — and therefore wages and employment

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Provincial Employment Standards

In labour economics we care how these rules change the decisions of workers and firms

And therefore how they change wages and employment

A great deal has been written about minimum wages in particular

We analyze them properly in Chapter 12

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Provincial Labour Relations

A separate piece of provincial legislation governs unionization and collective bargaining

Generally called the Labour Relations Act or Code

It defines:

The rules for forming a union
Expectations for negotiations between unionized employees and employers
Dispute resolution

This context helps explain differences across provinces in unionization rates and in unions’ ability to negotiate wages

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Equity and Human Rights

Several pieces of legislation protect workers’ rights and prevent discrimination







Employment Equity vs. Pay Equity


Employment equity requires employers to remove barriers to employment that disadvantage designated groups.
Pay equity requires employers to review compensation so women and men receive the same pay for work of equal value.




The Employment Equity Act applies in the federal jurisdiction

Designated groups: women, Aboriginal (Indigenous) Peoples, persons with disabilities, and members of visible minorities

Not all provinces have pay equity legislation, and coverage differs

The federal government introduced pay equity legislation in 2018

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Equity and Human Rights

The Canadian Human Rights Act applies to workplaces in the federal jurisdiction
It protects against discrimination based on:

Race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion
Age, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity or expression
Marital status, family status
Genetic characteristics, disability
A conviction for which a pardon has been granted

Each province has related legislation covering workers outside the federal jurisdiction







Tip


Discrimination is a large enough topic that we devote Chapter 15 to it.

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Types of Data
Labour economists catalogue data by the unit of observation.

Aggregate (time-series) — economy-wide measures like the unemployment rate, inflation, or GDP, reported over time
Cross-section microdata — earnings, hours, or education at the individual level at one point in time
Panel (longitudinal) — the same individuals followed over several periods

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Types of Data






2. Cross-section microdata


Variables such as earnings, hours of work, or education measured at the individual level at one point in time.




In Canada: the Census and the monthly Labour Force Survey
In the United States: the monthly Current Population Survey (CPS)

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Types of Data






3. Panel (longitudinal) data


Combines both — the same individuals followed over several time periods.




Lets us study dynamics: transitions into and out of the labour market
Lets us control for factors that are normally unobservable but fixed within a person

Motivation, for example — this matters a lot in Chapter 14

Few Canadian surveys are longitudinal, and access is restricted to protect privacy

Longitudinal Administrative Database (LAD) — tax records, following income over time
Canadian Employer–Employee Dynamics Database (CEEDD) — links firms to the individuals they employ
In the US: the PSID and the Health and Retirement Study

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Types of Data

The lines between these categories are increasingly blurred
Researchers combine multiple sources in a single analysis
“Big data” techniques bring in sources well beyond surveys:

Social media posts
Keywords in online job ads
Text analysis of media reports and Bank of Canada speeches








Tip


These newer sources often allow richer and more timely analysis than a survey released months after the fact.

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Introduction

The labour market involves several individual decisions about work

It is not simply whether to work or not

In the news you hear about statistics that quantify these decisions
In this section we cover the most common ones

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
The Labour Force Survey
The concepts above are measured by the Labour Force Survey (LFS).

Monthly survey run by Statistics Canada

Data readily available since 1976, administered since 1945

Samples about 68,000 households, yielding data on roughly 100,000 individuals aged 15 and over
Its main purpose is to produce the official unemployment rate used to administer Employment Insurance

We come back to EI in Chapter 5

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
The Labour Force Survey
Who is covered?

The eligible population is the civilian noninstitutional population aged 15 and over
Coverage excludes:

Reserves and other Indigenous settlements in the provinces
Extremely remote areas with very low population density


What can you get?

Public use microdata files (PUMFs) are freely available — a cross-section data set
The survey has a short longitudinal component: households are interviewed repeatedly for six months
Linkable confidential files are available to academic researchers

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
The Canadian Census

Conducted generally every five years; the most recent is 2021
Two parts:

A short form every household in Canada fills out
A long form with additional questions for a sample of Canadians

The 2021 Census describes circumstances in May 2021, including labour force status, and annual income in 2020
Labour economists use the Census to analyze annual earnings alongside characteristics not typically in the LFS

Ethnicity, language, country of birth








Note


The 2026 Census is administered in May 2026. Public use microdata files are expected two to three years later.

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
The Canadian Income Survey

An annual survey, similar in some ways to the LFS, but with much more detail on:

Annual earnings and other income sources
Family and demographic characteristics

This is the source behind the earnings distributions we looked at earlier in this section
Useful for describing how incomes differ between individual Canadians, not just on average

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Other Major Surveys

Some surveys focus on other domains but are still useful:

Canadian Community Health Survey — health
General Social Survey — social trends

Two more are central to describing the Canadian labour market:







Employer-side surveys


Survey of Employment, Payrolls, and Hours (SEPH) — businesses with at least one employee, combined with Canada Revenue Agency administrative data. Describes jobs, earnings, and hours within industries.
Job Vacancy and Wage Survey (JVWS) — describes job vacancies by occupation across geographies.




Microdata for these are not readily available outside Statistics Canada, given the sensitivity of the data

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
section: So You Want to Find the Data?
text:
So You Want to Find the Data?
Three routes are usually open to students at Canadian universities:

Statistics Canada

Search for a survey on their website and download any available PUMF

Data Liberation Initiative

Through your school’s library; PUMFs for academic research, plus some calculations on full data sets via real-time remote access (RTRA)

Research Data Centres Program

Approved researchers access hundreds of confidential microdata files not available to the public, in a secure environment








Tip


We will use PUMF data directly in this course — see the Introduction to R and Quarto material.

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Introduction

Labour economists rely on both theory and empirical research
Sometimes the evidence is a simple chart, graph, or table of means

Like the ones earlier in this section

More often we care about the relationship between variables

Then the evidence comes from regression analysis

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Correlation






Key Definition


The correlation coefficient describes the relationship between two variables, ranging from \(-1\) to \(1\).




Close to 1: strong positive · 0: none · close to -1: strong negative
Across countries, participation and log national income correlate at 0.28 for women and 0.41 for men

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Regression Analysis

Regression fits the line that best fits the data, rather than eyeballing it

\[\text{Participation rate} = a + b \times \ln(GNI) + e\]

Ordinary least squares chooses the line minimizing the sum of squared residuals
Estimating across 168 countries gives a slope of 4.12 for women

A one unit increase in log income is associated with a 4.12 percentage point higher participation rate

R-squared measures goodness of fit — income explains only 7.85% of the variation in women’s participation

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Regression Analysis
Estimating on 168 countries gives:
\[\text{Women's participation rate} = 18.62 + 4.12 \times \ln(GNI)\]

The coefficient 4.12 is the slope of the best-fit line

A one unit increase in log GNI is associated with a 4.12 percentage point increase in women’s participation

For men the slope is 3.52 — the line is slightly flatter

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Regression Analysis






R-squared


A measure of the goodness of fit of the regression — the share of variation in the outcome accounted for by the explanatory variables.




Income accounts for 16.8% of the variation in men’s participation across countries
But only 7.85% of the variation in women’s

Much more is needed to explain what we see across countries, particularly for women.

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Multiple Regression

We can add more variables. For the union wage differential:

\[\text{Weekly Earnings} = a + b\,\text{Unionized} + e\]

Adding controls for education, gender, age, and industry shrinks the differential
Adding job tenure shrinks it further — even negative in some provinces







Warning


But if a main role of unions is job security — letting people stay in higher-paying jobs — then controlling for tenure understates how much unions matter. Be careful what you control for.

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Multiple Regression: A Warning

Adding job tenure shrinks the union differential further — even negative in some provinces
But think about what that control is doing:

High-seniority employees earn more than new hires
They are also more likely to be unionized

What if a main role of unions is job security — letting people stay in higher-paying jobs rather than search for new ones?







Warning


“Adjusting” for job tenure then produces a coefficient that, if not carefully interpreted, understates how much unions matter for earnings. Be cautious interpreting multiple regression results.

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Correlation versus Causation

The number of movies Margot Robbie appears in correlates with the number of firefighters in South Dakota
The divorce rate in Maine correlates with margarine consumption in the United States







Key Definition


These are spurious correlations. A strong correlation does not mean one variable is causing changes in the other.




We usually want causal relationships, not just associations — which is what the next section is about

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Correlation versus Causation

So far we have only shown correlations between variables
Simple correlations interest labour economists, but more often we want:

Causal relationships
The precise mechanisms driving the outcomes we observe

Conducting causal research needs more statistical and econometric training than we offer here
But we can understand the research designs economists use — that is the next section







Tip


You will see these strategies throughout the course, in nearly every chapter’s empirical evidence.

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Introduction

Some questions are purely descriptive

Do workers with university degrees earn more than those with non-university postsecondary education? (They do — Chapter 14)

But we want to know whether university has a causal impact on wages
Perhaps people who go to university already had marketable skills learned in childhood

Those skills would have produced higher wages either way

We suspect confounding factors driving both wages and education decisions

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
The Fundamental Problem

University graduates earn more (Chapter 14) — but is that causal?

Perhaps they already had marketable skills that would have raised their wages anyway
We suspect confounding factors driving both wages and schooling








Key Definition


The counterfactual outcome is what would have happened to the treated had they not received the intervention. We can never observe it.

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
The Fundamental Problem
You injure your ankle, your doctor prescribes physiotherapy, and six weeks later it is healed.
Did the physiotherapy cause it to heal? Or would it have healed anyway?

You cannot answer this, because you cannot observe the healing that would have happened without treatment
Research designs are strategies for estimating that missing counterfactual







Why bother?


To design policy that addresses causes rather than symptoms, to predict what happens when conditions change, and to anticipate unintended consequences.

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
section: Why Do We Want Causal Estimates?
text:
Why Do We Want Causal Estimates?

For policy purposes, we want to address the underlying cause of a problem

Not merely treat its symptoms

We need causal relationships to predict future changes when underlying structural relationships change
We want to know how people and businesses respond to policy in ways that have unintended consequences

Which may be negative or positive

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Experimental and Nonexperimental Methods
Research designs are empirical strategies for estimating the counterfactual.






Experimental methods


Random assignment to treatment and control groups. The gold standard.




Two advantages:

We simply compare the mean outcomes of the two groups
They are easy to explain to, and be understood by, policymakers and the public

Nonexperimental methods use observational data

Limitations can be reduced with better data and careful use of multiple regression

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
section: And the Nobel Prize Goes to…
text:
And the Nobel Prize Goes to…

In 2021 the Canadian labour economist David Card was awarded the Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences for his empirical contributions to labour economics
He shared it with Joshua Angrist and Guido Imbens for their methodological contributions to the analysis of causal relationships







Note


Card’s minimum wage findings were initially met with real skepticism, because they did not line up with well-accepted theoretical predictions. His research has since prompted economists to re-examine the assumptions underlying those models — as we will see in Chapter 12.

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Audit and Resumé Studies






Key Definition


Audit studies approximate random assignment by comparing outcomes where the treatment is manipulated or hidden.




Resumé studies submit artificially manipulated resumés to real job ads and record which get call backs
Resumés are varied to signal demographic differences — common foreign versus domestic names, volunteer work signalling child care responsibilities, activities signalling sexual orientation

Several examples appear in Chapter 15.

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Before-and-After Comparison of Those Treated

Compares outcomes for the treated before and after the treatment
Requires longitudinal data, to follow the same individuals over time
Assumes pre-treatment outcomes are a good estimate of the counterfactual







Warning


This is often unconvincing. Consider a job search assistance program for recently unemployed workers. Comparing employment rates before and after will overstate the program’s impact, because some of those workers would have found jobs anyway.




Other things may also change between the two periods — economic conditions, for example
A more convincing design adds a comparison group of similar workers who did not participate

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
section: Post-Treatment Comparison of Treated and Comparison Groups
text:
Post-Treatment Comparison of Treated and Comparison Groups

Compares those who received the intervention to a similar group that did not
Requires only cross-section data on the two groups
Key assumption: the comparison group’s outcomes are a suitable estimate of the counterfactual

So choosing a comparison group as similar as possible is crucial

Without random assignment the groups will differ, so multiple regression controls for observable differences

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Post-Treatment Comparison: The Limitation

The problem is having no data before the intervention

Example: an education intervention — smaller class sizes, or adding teacher’s aides, to improve achievement test scores

We compare students in smaller classes to similar classes of regular size
But the comparison classes may have had different achievement levels before the intervention
Not accounting for those pre-treatment differences is likely to produce biased estimates

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Difference-in-Differences






Key Definition


Take both groups, before and after. Contrast each group’s change over time; the difference in those two differences estimates the causal effect.




This fixes the main limitations of both simpler designs
The comparison group’s change over time estimates the counterfactual







Tip


We use this twice: Maine vs New Brunswick in Chapter 5, and Card and Krueger in Chapter 12.

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
The Main Threat: Selection Bias

The threat is unobserved factors that influence which group someone is in and are correlated with the outcome

Regression controls cannot fix this, because the factors are unobserved








Key Definition


When people choose their own treatment status, we call it self-selection, or selection bias.



Example: a training program to improve skills and employability

Participants chose to apply; non-participants chose not to
They may have chosen on the basis of motivation or a desire to improve earnings — things the researcher cannot see
Those same factors also affect skills, employability, and earnings

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Natural Experiments






Key Definition


A natural experiment (or quasi-experiment) arises when some event affects some individuals and not others. Those affected are the treatment group; those not affected are the comparison group.




The event could be a policy change, a natural disaster, or any change in social or economic circumstances
Ideally the event occurs for exogenous reasons — unrelated to the treatment of interest
Then selection bias is not a problem, because those affected did not choose to be affected

Unobserved differences may still exist, but they are unrelated to the outcome

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Regression Discontinuity Designs

In many settings, receiving a treatment depends strictly on a score being above or below a threshold

Example: admission to a prestigious university requires scoring at least 92 percent on a competitive admission test

A student scoring 92 and a student scoring 91 are both excellent students

Perhaps one guessed a difficult question correctly and the other did not

But that tiny difference may have a large impact on future earnings

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Regression Discontinuity Designs

We would expect a jump, or discontinuity, in the relationship between future earnings and the admission score, right at the threshold
The size of that discontinuity estimates the treatment effect







Note


Like the post-treatment comparison, the RDD is a cross-sectional comparison. But it focuses on individuals who are otherwise very similar — nearly identical scores. That is why it is now so widely used in applied economics.

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Instrumental Variables

To get causal estimates from regression, the treatment variable must vary exogenously

Otherwise it changes because of confounding factors that also affect the outcome








Key Definition


The instrumental variable (IV) method finds a variable — an instrument — that affects the treatment variable exogenously, but does not affect the outcome directly.




The instrument must be uncorrelated with any other determinant of the outcome
This requirement is the exclusion restriction — the instrument is not directly in the equation relating the outcome to the treatment

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Instrumental Variables

The method uses only the variation in the treatment that is induced by the instrument

Example: using compulsory schooling laws as an instrument for education, to estimate the causal effect of additional education on earnings






Tip


This is exactly the strategy behind the compulsory schooling evidence in Chapter 14.

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Longitudinal Data and Fixed-Effects Estimators

Panel data let us follow the same individual over time
Useful for controlling selection bias from unobserved factors that are fixed within a person

Motivation, inherent intelligence, personality traits

Fixed-effect estimators identify causal effects from the changes a given individual makes in response to changes in the treatment variable







Tip


The twin studies in Chapter 14 work on this principle — comparing people who share what we cannot observe.

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
section: Propensity Score and Other Matching Procedures
text:
Propensity Score and Other Matching Procedures

The purpose of matching is to construct a control group to compare with the treatment group







Matching on observables


Build a control group that looks the same as the treatment group in terms of explanatory variables. They are like twins — except some received the treatment and others did not. The aim is to approximate random assignment.




Rather than matching on the variables directly, we can match on an index

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
section: Propensity Score and Other Matching Procedures
text:
Propensity Score and Other Matching Procedures






Key Definition


The propensity score is a function of the explanatory variables giving the probability of receiving treatment.



The steps:

Pool observations from the treatment and non-treatment groups
Estimate the probability of being in the treatment group
For each treated observation, calculate its estimated probability of being treated — its propensity score
Search the non-treated group for observations with the same or similar score

They look equally likely to have been treated — they simply were not.

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Synthetic Comparison Groups

Used when there is one treated group and several potential comparison groups
A synthetic comparison group is built from those potential groups

Chosen so their pre-treatment characteristics — both explanatory variables and outcomes — resemble the treatment group

Researchers place zero weight on the groups not used, and weight the others accordingly







Note


Instead of finding one comparison group that works, we build the best available one out of several imperfect ones.

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Research Designs: Summary



Design
Main worry




Audit / resumé studies
External validity


Before-and-after
No counterfactual


Post-treatment comparison
Pre-existing differences


Difference-in-differences
Selection bias


Natural experiment
Is the event really exogenous?


Regression discontinuity
Effects only near the cut-off


Instrumental variables
Exclusion restriction


Fixed effects
Only handles fixed unobservables


Matching / propensity score
Unobservables remain


Synthetic comparison
Pre-treatment fit

title: EC306 - Wages and Employment
text:
Summary

Participation varies enormously across countries, and most of that variation is in women’s participation
Which employment law applies to you depends on your employer’s industry, not where you live
The LFS, Census, and CIS are the workhorses; the LFS defines every unemployment number you hear
A regression coefficient is not automatically a causal effect
Estimating a causal effect means estimating a counterfactual we can never observe — every research design is a different way of building one

When you see evidence in this course, ask what the comparison group is, and whether you believe it.
